scene.testo: Imagine you are strapped into a seat, falling toward Earth at 17,500 miles per hour. Outside your window, the air turns into a river of fire. It burns at about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit. And you cannot do a single thing about it.

This is re-entry. For months, astronauts live in orbit about 250 miles above Earth. They float, they work, they laugh. But every one of them knows the ride home is the most dangerous part of the whole mission.

By the end of this video, you will understand why. Not because the machines are weak, but because of something stranger. Re-entry gives you almost no second chances. And the history of spaceflight proves it, in ways NASA never forgot.

Here is the first clue. Getting to orbit takes a rocket. But getting home needs no engine at all. Gravity does the pulling. Your only job is to survive the air. And air, at that speed, behaves like a wall.

Start with the speed. A spacecraft in low Earth orbit moves at about 17,500 miles per hour. That is roughly 5 miles every second. At that pace, you could cross the entire state of Texas in under two minutes.
To land, a spacecraft has to throw away almost all of that speed. A rocket burn slows it just enough to drop out of orbit. The burn lasts only a few minutes. But after it, there is no turning back.

Then comes the edge of the atmosphere. Engineers call it entry interface, at about 400,000 feet up. That is roughly 76 miles high. The air there is incredibly thin. But at 17,500 miles per hour, even thin air starts to hurt.

Here is what really happens. The spacecraft does not burn like a match. It slams into air molecules faster than they can move away. The air in front gets crushed, and crushed air gets hot. Extremely hot.

The space shuttle faced temperatures of up to about 3,000 degrees Fahrenheit on its underside. That is around 1,650 degrees Celsius. Hot enough to melt steel, and hot enough to glow brighter than a campfire.

Now imagine you are inside. The cabin is quiet at first. Then you feel a gentle push into your seat. Through the window, a faint orange glow appears. Within a minute, the glow turns into a wall of fire.

Astronauts have described that glow in their own words. Pink, orange, and sometimes bright white light flickering outside the windows. It looks beautiful, and that is the strange part. The most dangerous minutes of the flight are also the most colorful.

And then, the radio goes silent. The plasma around the spacecraft blocks radio signals. For several minutes, Mission Control cannot hear a word. This is called the communications blackout. For the Apollo missions, it lasted about three minutes.

Picture the control room during that silence. Dozens of engineers staring at screens. Nobody talking. Nobody able to help. If something goes wrong inside that plasma, they will not know until it is already over.

Now add the weight. As the spacecraft hits thicker air, it slows down fast. Fast braking means heavy force. Space shuttle crews felt about 3 times their normal weight, called 3 Gs. Apollo crews coming home from the Moon felt much more.

Think about what that means. After months of floating, your body forgets weight. Suddenly, your arms feel like lead. Your head feels like a bowling ball. And you must still read dials and flip switches.

Long stays in orbit make this worse. Bones and muscles weaken in weightlessness. Doctors have documented that astronauts on the space station lose bone density over months. So the body is at its weakest exactly when gravity returns.

But the biggest fear is not the heat or the weight. It is the angle. A spacecraft must hit the atmosphere at a very narrow angle. Too steep, and it burns up or crushes the crew. Too shallow, and it bounces off.

Engineers call that target the re-entry corridor. For the Apollo capsules returning from the Moon, the corridor was only a few degrees wide. Miss it by a small amount, and the mission could end in disaster.

That is why the first American crews to go to the Moon trusted their lives to careful math. Every burn, every second, every tiny push of the thrusters mattered. There was no room for guessing on the way home.

And the heat shield was the last line of defense. It sat on the bottom of the capsule, a thick layer of special material designed to burn away slowly. As it burned, it carried the heat off into the air.
Yes, the shield was meant to burn. It was built to char and flake off, piece by piece. That sounds scary, but it worked. The material took the punishment so the astronauts would not.

The space shuttle used a different trick. Its belly was covered with about 24,000 heat-resistant tiles, plus special panels on the nose and wing edges. Each tile was made mostly of silica, and each one was installed by hand.

Those tiles had a strange property. A tile fresh from a furnace could be held by its edges with bare fingers, even while its center glowed red. NASA demonstrated this many times. The material barely carried heat.

But tiles were fragile. A small dent or crack could matter. Every shuttle landing was followed by a careful inspection, tile by tile. Workers spent weeks checking and replacing damaged pieces before the next flight.

That fragility led to the darkest day in modern re-entry history. February 1, 2003. The space shuttle Columbia was returning from a 16-day science mission. Seven astronauts were on board. They were about 16 minutes from home.

During launch, 16 days earlier, a piece of foam insulation had broken off the external tank. It struck the left wing at high speed. Engineers saw it on video. But nobody knew how bad the damage really was.

The investigation later found the foam had punched a hole in the wing's leading edge. During re-entry, superheated gas entered through that hole. It melted the wing from the inside. Sensors began failing, one after another.

At about 200,000 feet over Texas, Columbia broke apart. It was traveling at roughly 12,500 miles per hour. The crew was lost. Debris fell across a path of land hundreds of miles long, and thousands of people searched for it.

That day changed NASA. Inspections became stricter. Crews began checking the shuttle's heat shield in orbit, using a long boom with cameras and sensors. They also kept a second shuttle ready for rescue on later missions.

Columbia was not the first warning. In 1967, a fire killed three Apollo 1 astronauts on the ground. And in 1986, the shuttle Challenger was lost during launch. Re-entry carries its own risks, and its own long list of lessons.

But history also holds a story of survival. April 1970. Apollo 13. An oxygen tank exploded two days into the trip to the Moon. The crew of three had to swing around the Moon and fly home in a damaged ship.

They spent days in a cold, cramped lunar module, used as a lifeboat. Temperatures inside dropped close to freezing. Water was rationed. Sleep was nearly impossible. And all of it led to one final test, re-entry.

Nobody knew if the heat shield had survived the explosion. Engineers on the ground could only hope. On April 17, 1970, the capsule hit the atmosphere. The blackout lasted longer than expected, and the control room waited in silence.

Then three parachutes opened over the Pacific Ocean. The crew was alive. Splashdown, followed by cheers in Mission Control. The heat shield had held. A very close call, and one of the great rescues in spaceflight history.

So the fear is not only about heat. It is also about everything that must work after it. Parachutes must open. Thrusters must fire. Computers must stay calm. One weak link breaks the chain, and the whole mission fails.

Even the Soyuz, one of the most reliable spacecraft ever flown, has had its scary moments. Its capsule has landed far off target before, because of steep descents. Crews have reported strong forces and rough landings in documented accounts.

A Soyuz landing is a controlled crash. Parachutes slow the capsule to around 20 feet per second. Then small rockets fire just above the ground to soften the touchdown. Astronauts describe it as a hard jolt, like a car crash.

Modern capsules, like SpaceX Dragon, splash down in the ocean. The capsule drops under four big parachutes at about 15 miles per hour. Recovery boats rush in. Still, the crew goes through the same fire first.

And then comes the weirdest part. Back on Earth, the body struggles to stand. Astronauts often feel dizzy. Some cannot walk straight for hours. They are carried from the capsule in chairs, and doctors check them within minutes.

Compare that with your life on Earth. A car braking on the highway might slow you from 70 miles per hour to zero. A spacecraft must lose about 250 times that speed, in about 30 minutes, through a sky of fire.
A football field is 100 yards long. At 17,500 miles per hour, a spacecraft covers that distance in about 0.03 seconds. So you could blink once, and the capsule would cross dozens of football fields.

So why do astronauts fear re-entry more than anything else? Because launch has abort systems, and orbit has time to fix problems. But in re-entry, there is no pause button. Physics takes over, and it does not negotiate.

And yet, here is the most surprising detail. After everything, the fire and the force and the silence, astronauts keep going back. Hundreds of people have returned safely. Fear is real, but so is trust in the people who built the ship.

descrizione:
Why do astronauts fear re-entry more than anything else? In this Orbital Days documentary, we ride a spacecraft from 250 miles above Earth at 17,500 mph down through a wall of plasma that reaches about 3,000°F.

We look at the heat shield, the communications blackout, the narrow re-entry corridor, the Columbia accident on February 1, 2003, and the Apollo 13 return on April 17, 1970. Every fact comes from NASA records and documented astronaut accounts.

If you love space station life, NASA history, and real spaceflight science, subscribe to Orbital Days for more stories from orbit.
